questions.text: What is the AAMA Gold Label structural resistance rating for windows?

options.text: 50 mph wind pressure, suitable for areas with moderate wind exposure and standard building codes
75 mph wind pressure, designed for regions with higher wind speeds and more stringent safety requirements
120 mph wind pressure, applicable to hurricane-prone zones requiring enhanced structural integrity

rationale.a: 50 mph is inadequate for any commercial application.
rationale.b: 75 mph is lower than Gold Label; suitable for standard-grade windows.
rationale.d: 120 mph exceeds Gold Label and would require specialized storm-resistant construction.
rationale.correct: AAMA Gold Label windows must resist at least 94 mph wind pressure without failure, the highest structural rating.
rationale.takeaway: AAMA Gold Label = ≥94 mph structural resistance. For typhoon zones exceeding 150 mph, specify reinforced frames or storm glazing.

questions.text: A coastal building in the Philippines experiences frequent salt spray. What window hardware material should be specified to resist corrosion?

options.text: Painted steel, which may require frequent maintenance due to corrosion
Standard aluminum, which is prone to corrosion in salty environments
Galvanized steel, which offers some protection but may not be sufficient in severe conditions

rationale.a: Painted steel loses its coating in salt spray, exposing the steel to corrosion.
rationale.b: Standard aluminum corrodes through pitting in salt spray; galvanic corrosion occurs when aluminum contacts steel.
rationale.d: Galvanized steel offers some protection but is inferior to stainless steel in salt spray.
rationale.correct: Salt spray rapidly corrodes painted steel and standard aluminum. Stainless steel (preferably 304 or 316 marine grade) or coated aluminum (powder-coated or anodized) resist corrosion in coastal environments.
rationale.takeaway: Coastal projects = stainless steel or coated aluminum hardware. Never specify standard painted or uncoated metals.

questions.explanation: Painted steel loses its coating in salt spray, exposing the steel to corrosion. Galvanized steel offers some protection but is inferior to stainless steel in salt spray. Salt spray rapidly corrodes painted steel and standard aluminum. Stainless steel (preferably 304 or 316 marine grade) or coated aluminum (powder-coated or anodized) resist corrosion in coastal environments. Coastal projects = stainless steel or coated aluminum hardware. Never specify standard painted or uncoated metals.

questions.text: Which window type automatically sheds rain while allowing ventilation through the bottom opening?

rationale.a: Fixed windows do not open; they provide no ventilation.
rationale.b: Sliding windows do not shed rain effectively; water can enter around the sash during heavy rain.
rationale.c: Casement windows open to the full width but do not automatically shed rain.
rationale.correct: Awning windows hinge at the top and swing outward at the bottom. This design naturally sheds rain while the bottom opening allows air intake, ideal for humid climates.
rationale.takeaway: Awning windows = hinge top, open bottom, rain shedding. Ideal for tropical and monsoon-prone regions.

Ideal for tropical and monsoon-prone regions.

questions.text: What is the primary function of weatherstripping in a window assembly?

options.text: To support the weight of the sash, ensuring it remains in place during operation
To reduce air leakage and water infiltration around the sash
To provide aesthetic trim, enhancing the visual appeal of the window
To prevent the sash from sticking, allowing for smooth operation

rationale.a: Sash support is provided by hinges, balance mechanisms, or friction stays.
rationale.c: Aesthetic trim is a secondary function; the primary purpose is sealing.
rationale.d: Lubricants or track design prevent sticking, not weatherstripping.
rationale.correct: Weatherstripping seals the gap between the sash and frame, reducing air leakage by 30-50 percent and preventing water infiltration during rain.
rationale.takeaway: Weatherstripping = leakage reduction (30-50%) + water prevention. Essential for tropical climates with monsoons.

questions.text: What is the AAMA Gold Label air leakage limit for windows?

rationale.a: 0.50 cfm exceeds Gold Label (≤0.30 cfm) limit but may pass lower performance classes.
rationale.c: 0.15 cfm is an exceptional limit not defined in standard AAMA grading.
rationale.d: 1.00 cfm is far too high for any AAMA-certified window.
rationale.correct: AAMA Gold Label windows are limited to 0.30 cfm (cubic feet per minute) at 25 mph wind speed, the highest performance tier.
rationale.takeaway: AAMA Gold Label = ≤0.30 cfm air leakage. Always specify Gold Label for tropical and typhoon-prone regions.

questions.text: A window currently has an air leakage rate of 0.50 cfm at 25 mph. After installing high-quality weatherstripping that reduces air leakage by 40 percent, what is the new air leakage rate?

rationale.a: 0.10 cfm would require an even greater reduction (80 percent).
rationale.b: 0.20 cfm would require a 60 percent reduction.
rationale.d: 0.40 cfm does not meet AAMA Gold Label (≤0.30 cfm).
rationale.correct: New air leakage = 0.50 cfm × (1 - 0.40) = 0.50 × 0.60 = 0.30 cfm, which meets AAMA Gold Label requirements.
rationale.takeaway: Use the formula: New leakage = Original × (1 - reduction percent). Verify that the result meets AAMA Gold Label (≤0.30 cfm).

questions.text: During LEA exam analysis, a residential project in Areas with PAGASA Signal No. 4+ (winds exceeding 150 kph gusts) specifies standard AAMA windows (not Gold Label) with 94 mph structural resistance. Why is this specification inadequate, and what should be specified instead?

options.text: Standard AAMA is sufficient; the 94 mph rating covers the project needs, assuming no extreme weather conditions are expected
Standard AAMA windows have only 94 mph rating, but typhoon gusts can exceed 150 mph. Upgraded windows, reinforced frames, or storm-resistant glazing and framing must be specified.
The problem is air leakage, not structural resistance; weatherstripping will solve it, although it does not address the core issue of structural integrity
AAMA Gold Label (94 mph) is equivalent to standard AAMA; there is no difference, which is a common misconception

rationale.a: 94 mph is insufficient for 150+ mph typhoons; structural failure is likely.
rationale.c: Air leakage is a separate concern; the structural issue is wind resistance.
rationale.d: Both are AAMA certified, but Gold Label has superior air leakage performance; the issue here is structural resistance beyond Gold Label capability.
rationale.correct: Typhoon Zone 1 can exceed 150 mph; standard AAMA windows (94 mph) will fail. Either upgrade to windows rated for higher wind speeds, reinforce the frame with impact-resistant materials, or use storm-resistant glazing and framing systems.
rationale.takeaway: For extreme wind zones, AAMA Gold Label (94 mph) may be insufficient. Verify local wind speeds and specify accordingly.

questions.text: A friction stay in a window is rated to hold 50 lbf at 70°F. The temperature coefficient is -0.75 percent per degree Fahrenheit. At an ambient temperature of 95°F, what is the approximate holding force?

rationale.a: 37.5 lbf assumes a reduction of 25 percent (1.0% per °F), which is too aggressive.
rationale.c: 42.5 lbf assumes only a 15 percent reduction, underestimating the temperature effect.
rationale.d: 48.1 lbf assumes only a 3.8 percent reduction, too small for a 25°F swing.
rationale.correct: Temperature change = 95°F - 70°F = 25°F. Force reduction = 50 lbf × 0.0075 × 25 = 9.375 lbf. Holding force = 50 - 9.375 = 40.625 ≈ 40.6 lbf.
rationale.takeaway: Friction stay strength decreases with temperature. Always account for peak ambient temperature in tropical climates when specifying hardware.

questions.text: What is the typical force required to operate a casement window crank?

rationale.a: 5 lbf is too light; the operator may not have sufficient mechanical advantage.
rationale.b: 10 lbf is lighter than typical; 15 lbf is more common.
rationale.d: 30 lbf exceeds the comfort limit and creates accessibility issues for elderly or disabled users.
rationale.correct: Casement window cranks typically require approximately 15 lbf of force, with a crank arm length of 10-12 inches. This is the ergonomic limit for comfortable operation.
rationale.takeaway: Casement crank force ≈ 15 lbf with 10-12 inch arm. Longer arms reduce the force required.

questions.text: What is the maximum water infiltration rate at 15 mph wind speed (2.86 psf static pressure) for AAMA Gold Label windows?

options.text: Light water penetration acceptable if dried within 1 hour
Up to 5 percent of test surface allowed to leak

rationale.a: Gold Label allows no water penetration; lower grades may allow light penetration.
rationale.b: Time-to-dry is not a criterion; no water should enter.
rationale.d: Gold Label specifies zero infiltration, not a percentage-based allowance.
rationale.correct: AAMA Gold Label windows must resist water infiltration up to 32 mph without any water entering the building interior. This is a zero-tolerance standard.
rationale.takeaway: AAMA Gold Label water resistance = zero infiltration at 32 mph. Anything else fails the test.
